---

## Key Princi...
lessons.content_md:
# Do's and Don'ts of Mockup Design **Reading & Practical Guide · 10 Minutes** Creating intuitive, professional mockups is the bridge between conceptual sketches and coded frontends. Here is a definitive guide to best practices and common anti-patterns in modern interface design. --- ## Key Principles of High-Converting Mockups | Aspect | The Do's (Best Practices) | The Don'ts (Common Traps) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Visual Hierarchy** | Use clear scale, font weights, and spacing so the user's eye lands on the primary CTA within 3 seconds. | Don't give every button equal weight or vibrant color, causing visual competition. | | **Grid & Alignment** | Stick to an 8pt or 4pt grid system across all margins, paddings, and component heights. | Don't eyeball spacing or use arbitrary values like 13px or 27px padding. | | **Color Usage** | Limit your palette to 1 primary brand color, 1 neutral dark, 1 neutral light, and functional alert tones (green/red/amber). | Don't use more than 3 accent colors or saturated neons that strain eye comfort. | | **Typography** | Pair at most two typefaces (e.g., Space Grotesk for Headings + DM Sans for Body); maintain 1.4-1.6 line height. | Don't use more than 2 distinct font families or line heights below 1.2 on body copy. | | **Form Design** | Keep input labels visible above fields, provide clear placeholder hints, and show inline validation feedback. | Don't rely solely on disappearing placeholders as the only label for input fields. | | **Realism in Data** | Use realistic, localized user names, product titles, and numbers to test real-world overflow. | Don't rely on repetitive "Lorem Ipsum" or names that are always 4 letters long. | --- ## 5 Critical Rules Before Handoff to Development 1. **Design System Consistency:** Ensure every button, input, and card is an instance of a master component in Figma. 2. **Auto Layout Discipline:** Group items with Auto Layout (Flexbox logic) so elements reflow responsively across device sizes. 3. **Empty & Error States:** Always design empty states ("No courses enrolled yet") and error states ("Payment timeout") rather than only happy paths. 4. **Touch Target Sizing:** Ensure every interactive mobile button has a minimum tap target of **44x44 points** (iOS HIG) or **48x48 dp** (Material Design). 5. **Dark Mode Contrast:** When designing dark themes, use dark slate or charcoal (#0F172A / #18181B) rather than pure #000000 to prevent harsh contrast halation.

I'm a student learning web dev. I prefer short,
practical explanations with code examples and a
challenge after each topic. I'm from India — use ₹.
```

lessons.title: 13. Beginner's Guide to Design Thinking
lessons.description: A deep dive into empathizing with user pain points and developing actionable problem statements.
lessons.content_md:
**Reading: Beginner’s Guide to Design Thinking Estimated Time: 20 mins Learning objectives:** After completing this reading, you will be able to: Provide a beginner-friendly explanation of what Design Thinking is and why it's important for problem-solving and innovation Break down the five stages of Design Thinking—Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test—in a simple and relatable way Illustrate each stage with real-life examples Emphasize the benefits of Design Thinking, including user-centered solutions, innovation, risk reduction, and collaboration “Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones.” - Herbert Simon https://cf-courses-data.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/mBDs7GtFY58W8u-uUedy\_Q/herbert-simon-.jpg Introduction to Design Thinking Design Thinking is a powerful, user-centered approach to problem-solving that helps businesses and designers create innovative solutions tailored to the needs of their users. It's not just a process; it's a mindset that prioritizes empathy, creativity, and iteration. In this guide, we'll break down the Design Thinking process, explore its stages with real-life examples, and provide creative insights to help you apply it in your own projects. Let's talk about morning scenario Think of the last time you had tea, coffee, or hot cocoa. Maybe it was this morning. How did it make you feel? Why did you drink it? What else were you doing at the time? Chances are your answers to those questions are different than anyone else who drank a hot beverage recently. Those answers represent your experience. https://cf-courses-data.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/XNbNTEeHr254dFF\_dEbkKA/hot-beverage-.jpg The 5 stages of design https://cf-courses-data.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/bsl2L1x1vSUFukebIFfrfw/Heading.png 1. Empathize: Understanding the user The first step is to put yourself in the user's shoes. This means observing, engaging, and empathizing with your target audience to understand their needs, motivations, and pain points. Without empathy, you risk designing solutions that don't truly address user problems. Here's a deeper dive into how to conduct user research effectively, with actionable steps: 1.1. Talk to users: Conduct interviews One of the most direct ways to empathize with users is by talking to them. Interviews allow you to ask open-ended questions and dig deeper into their experiences. 1.2. Observe user behavior: Contextual inquiry Sometimes, what users say and what they do can differ. Observing users in their natural environment helps you understand their actual behaviors and challenges. 1.3. Map the user journey A user journey map is a visual representation of the steps users take to achieve a goal. It helps you identify pain points and opportunities for improvement. 1.4. Use surveys and questionnaires Surveys are a great way to gather quantitative data from a larger audience. They help you identify patterns and trends in user behavior. 1.5. Create empathy maps An empathy map is a tool that helps you visualize what users say, think, feel, and do. It's a great way to synthesize research findings and build a deeper understanding of your users. 1.6. Shadow users Shadowing involves following users as they go about their daily routines. It's particularly useful for understanding complex workflows or behaviors. 1.7. Analyze existing data Sometimes, valuable insights are already available in your organization's data. Look at customer support logs, app analytics, or social media feedback to identify common issues. Real-Life example of empathize: Imagine you're designing a fitness app. Instead of assuming what users want, you conduct interviews and surveys to understand their fitness goals, challenges, and preferences. You might discover that users struggle with staying motivated or finding time to exercise. This insight becomes the foundation for your design. 2\. Define: Framing the problem Once you've gathered insights, the next step is to define the core problem. This involves synthesizing your research and articulating the challenge from the user's perspective. Real-life example: Using the fitness app scenario, you might define the problem as: "Busy professionals need a quick, motivating way to incorporate exercise into their daily routines because they struggle to find time for long workouts.” 3\. Ideate: Generating creative solutions This is the brainstorming phase where you generate a wide range of ideas to solve the defined problem. The goal is to think outside the box and explore unconventional solutions. Real-life example: For the fitness app, you might brainstorm ideas such as: A 15-minute workout challenge with rewards A feature that syncs with user's calendars to suggest workout times 4\. Prototype: Bringing ideas to life Prototyping involves creating tangible representations of your ideas. These can range from low-fidelity sketches to interactive digital mockups. Start with paper prototypes to quickly test ideas before investing time in digital tools. For example, sketch out the app's interface on paper and simulate user interactions by hand. Prototypes are essential tools in the design process, allowing designers to test ideas and gather feedback before investing in full development. There are two main types of prototypes, each serving a different purpose: Low-fidelity prototypes Low-fidelity (lo-fi) prototypes are simple, rough representations of a design. They focus on the basic structure and functionality rather than visuals. https://cf-courses-data.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/IJH7m3NFEW8avi4g82E9RQ/image%20-5-.png High-fidelity prototypes High-fidelity (hi-fi) prototypes are more polished and interactive, closely resembling the final product. They include detailed visuals, animations, and sometimes even functional elements. https://cf-courses-data.s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/DirOT-0pndunhnjLMOMiQg/image%20-6-.png Real-life example: For the fitness app, you might create a low-fidelity wireframe of the app's homepage, showing the layout of workout options, a progress tracker, and a rewards section. You could then develop a clickable prototype using tools such as Figma or Adobe XD. 5\. Test: Gathering feedback and iterating The final stage involves testing your prototypes with real users to gather feedback and identify areas for improvement. This stage often leads to new insights, requiring you to revisit earlier stages. Real-life example: You test the fitness app prototype with a group of busy professionals. They love the 15-minute workout idea but find the navigation confusing. Based on their feedback, you simplify the interface and add a tutorial for first-time users. Testing isn't a one-time step: The iterative nature of Design Thinking In Design Thinking, testing is not the final destination—it's a critical part of an ongoing, iterative process. The feedback you gather during testing often leads you back to earlier stages, such as brainstorming or prototyping, to refine and improve your solution. This cyclical approach ensures that the final product truly meets user needs. Benefits of Design Thinking User-centered solutions: By focusing on user needs, you create products that are intuitive and valuable. Encourages innovation: The iterative process fosters creativity and out-of-the-box thinking. Reduces risk: Testing prototypes early helps identify issues before launching the final product. Promotes collaboration: Design Thinking brings together diverse perspectives, leading to better solutions. Real-life applications of Design Thinking 1\. Airbnb: Redefining the travel experience Airbnb used Design Thinking to transform its platform. By empathizing with users, they discovered that travelers wanted more than just a place to stay—they wanted unique, local experiences. This insight led to features such as "Experiences" and personalized recommendations, which revolutionized the travel industry. 2\. Netflix: Enhancing user experience Netflix constantly uses Design Thinking to improve its platform. Through user research, they discovered that viewers often struggled to decide what to watch. This led to the development of personalized recommendations and a seamless, intuitive interface. 3\. Healthcare: Patient-centered solutions Example: GE Healthcare – Infant Warmer Challenge: In developing countries, premature babies often die due to a lack of incubators. Design Thinking Approach: GE Healthcare used empathy-driven research to understand the needs of rural clinics. Solution: Developed a low-cost, easy-to-use infant warmer (Embrace Warmer) instead of a traditional incubator. This portable device functions without electricity and is cost-effective, helping save newborn lives. 4\. Education: Personalized learning Example: Duolingo – Gamified language learning Challenge: Traditional language learning methods were tedious and ineffective for many learners. Design Thinking Approach: Duolingo leveraged user feedback, iterative prototyping, and A/B testing to refine its app. Solution: A gamified, bite-sized learning experience that adapts to individual users’ learning speeds and preferences, increasing engagement and retention. 5\. Retail: Enhancing customer experience Example: Nike – Customizable shoes (Nike By You) Challenge: Customers wanted more personalized shopping experiences. Design Thinking Approach: Nike engaged customers through surveys, tested different interactive shopping experiences, and refined designs based on feedback. Solution: Nike By You, a service allowing customers to design their own shoes, increasing engagement and customer satisfaction.

Recommended video

What Is Design Thinking? An Overview — AJ&Smart

lessons.description:
# Practice Quiz: Responsive Web Design (RWD)
**Practice Quiz · 10 Minutes · 5 Questions**

Validate your understanding of media queries, viewport meta tags, relative units, and responsive images.

---

### Question 1
**What is the purpose of the `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, in...
lessons.content_md:
# Practice Quiz: Responsive Web Design (RWD) **Practice Quiz · 10 Minutes · 5 Questions** Validate your understanding of media queries, viewport meta tags, relative units, and responsive images. --- ### Question 1 **What is the purpose of the `` HTML tag?** - A) It optimizes images for high-DPI retina screens. - B) It instructs mobile browsers to render the page at the physical width of the device screen rather than scaling down a 980px desktop canvas. - C) It triggers hardware acceleration on CSS animations. - D) It enables offline PWA caching automatically. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers assume the page is designed for desktop and scale it down into a tiny, unreadable 980px canvas that requires pinch-to-zoom. --- ### Question 2 **Which CSS unit is relative to the root element's font size, making it ideal for scalable typography and consistent rem-based design systems?** - A) px - B) em - C) rem - D) vh * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** `rem` stands for "Root EM". It scales relative to the `` root font size (usually 16px by default), allowing users who adjust their browser accessibility font sizes to see the entire site scale cleanly. --- ### Question 3 **In modern CSS, which function allows you to define a fluid value that stays between a minimum and maximum bound based on viewport width?** - A) `calc(100% - 20px)` - B) `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2.5rem)` - C) `minmax(200px, 1fr)` - D) `scale(1.2)` * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** `clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX)` clamps an ideal value (often using viewport units like `vw`) between an accessible floor and ceiling without needing multiple media query lines. --- ### Question 4 **What distinguishes a "Fluid Layout" from an "Adaptive Layout"?** - A) Fluid layouts use percentages or fractional units (`fr`) to resize continuously, while adaptive layouts jump between fixed widths at specific media query breakpoints. - B) Fluid layouts only work on iOS devices. - C) Adaptive layouts do not use CSS. - D) Fluid layouts require JavaScript resize listeners. * **Correct Answer:** A * **Explanation:** Fluid design scales continuously like liquid filling a container. Adaptive design loads distinct fixed layouts at discrete width thresholds. --- ### Question 5 **What is the CSS media query condition to detect if a user prefers reduced motion for accessibility?** - A) `@media (pointer: coarse)` - B) `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` - C) `@media (color-gamut: p3)` - D) `@media (display-mode: standalone)` * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` allows designers and developers to disable or tone down dramatic animations for vestibular-disorder-sensitive users.

lessons.title: Slides + Calendar Team Coordination
lessons.description:
## First Understanding

- **Slides** = collaborative decks with shared themes; **Calendar** = the team's shared time.
- Slides live in Drive and embed Docs/Sheets/charts — one source of truth.
- Calendar blocking (focus time, prep time) is a professional habit, not selfishness.## First Understanding

- **Slides** = collaborative decks with shared themes; **Calendar** = the team's shared time.
- Slides live in Drive and embed Docs/Sheets/charts — one source of truth.
- Calendar blocking (focus time, prep time) is a professional habit, not selfishness.Meetings and decks run on these two apps.

## Slides speed
- Explore → AI-generated layouts from bullets
- Ctrl+D duplicate · F5 present
- Insert → Speaker notes + live captions (CC)

## Calendar power moves
- Create event → check "Add Google Meet" → link auto-sent
- "Find a time" → see when everyone is free
- Focus time blocks for deep work
- Multiple calendars (work/personal/team) with colors

> [!tip] Calendar is a promise. Show, don't just tell: block 1 hour daily for focused learning.

## Suggestions and Tips

- Insert live charts from Sheets so slides never go stale.
- Set up **focus time** blocks — they protect the deep work meetings steal.
- Use Calendar's 'Speedy meetings' to end at :25/:55 — respect everyone's buffer.

lessons.description:
# Practice Quiz: Introduction to Design
**Estimated Time:** 10 Minutes · **Total Questions:** 5 · **Passing Score:** 80%

Test your foundational understanding of UI vs. UX design, design thinking phases, and user-centered design principles.

---

### Question 1
**What is the primary distinction betw...
lessons.content_md:
# Practice Quiz: Introduction to Design **Estimated Time:** 10 Minutes · **Total Questions:** 5 · **Passing Score:** 80% Test your foundational understanding of UI vs. UX design, design thinking phases, and user-centered design principles. --- ### Question 1 **What is the primary distinction between UI (User Interface) and UX (User Experience) design?** - A) UI focuses on how a product feels and solves user problems; UX focuses on graphic design and colors. - B) UI deals with the aesthetic, visual elements and interactive touchpoints; UX encompasses the overall user journey, ergonomics, and problem-solving experience. - C) UI is only for mobile applications, while UX is exclusively for desktop websites. - D) UI is handled entirely by backend software engineers, while UX is done by marketing. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** UI (User Interface) focuses on the visual presentation, typography, colors, and layout that users interact with directly. UX (User Experience) is broader, encompassing user research, information architecture, workflow efficiency, and satisfaction throughout the entire user journey. --- ### Question 2 **Which stage of the 5-stage Design Thinking process focuses on formulating a clear, actionable problem statement based on user research?** - A) Empathize - B) Ideate - C) Define - D) Prototype * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** In the **Define** phase, designers synthesize their findings from the Empathize phase to pinpoint the core problems and formulate a human-centered Problem Statement (e.g., "Point of View" or POV). --- ### Question 3 **Which visual design principle ensures that elements that belong together are placed close to one another, helping users mentally group information?** - A) Hierarchy - B) Contrast - C) Proximity - D) Repetition * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** The principle of **Proximity** (one of the Gestalt laws) states that objects placed near each other are perceived as a single unified group, reducing cognitive load for the user. --- ### Question 4 **Why is Wireframing considered an essential early step before diving into high-fidelity Figma mockups?** - A) It allows designers and stakeholders to focus on structure, content layout, and information flow without being distracted by colors and imagery. - B) It generates automated CSS code ready for production deployment. - C) It replaces the need for user testing. - D) It enforces brand typography rules automatically. * **Correct Answer:** A * **Explanation:** Low-fidelity wireframes strip away visual distractions like color palettes and photography so the team can validate information hierarchy, navigation clarity, and functionality first. --- ### Question 5 **What is the WCAG recommended contrast ratio for normal body text against its background to ensure accessibility (AA standard)?** - A) 1.5:1 - B) 3.0:1 - C) 4.5:1 - D) 10:1 * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 AA level requires a contrast ratio of at least **4.5:1** for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt or 14pt bold).

lessons.content_md:
# Practice Quiz: Figma Introduction **Practice Quiz · 10 Minutes · 5 Questions** Assess your foundational knowledge of Figma canvas tools, keyboard shortcuts, frames, and vectors. --- ### Question 1 **What is the keyboard shortcut to automatically add Auto Layout to a group of selected layers in Figma?** - A) `Ctrl + G` (or `Cmd + G`) - B) `Shift + A` - C) `Ctrl + Alt + K` - D) `Spacebar + A` * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** `Shift + A` applies Auto Layout to the selected layers, immediately converting them into a flexible flexbox-style container. --- ### Question 2 **What is the key difference between a "Group" and a "Frame" in Figma?** - A) Groups can contain Auto Layout, whereas Frames cannot. - B) Frames act as independent canvas artboards with their own dimensions, constraints, and clipping rules; Groups simply bundle layers together based on the bounding box of their children. - C) Groups are only for vector paths. - D) Frames cannot contain text. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** A Frame is an autonomous layout container with explicit dimensions, constraints, auto layout, and clipping abilities. Groups have no independent dimensions and shrink/grow based on their children. --- ### Question 3 **Which icon indicates a Master Component in Figma vs. an Instance?** - A) A solid diamond (`◆`) vs. a hollow diamond (`◇`) - B) Four filled diamonds forming a larger diamond (`❖`) represents a Master Component; a single hollow diamond (`◇`) represents an Instance. - C) A folder icon vs. a file icon. - D) A circle vs. a square. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** In Figma's layer panel, the 4-diamond symbol (`❖`) denotes a Master Component. An Instance is represented by a single outline diamond (`◇`). --- ### Question 4 **When designing a responsive component in Auto Layout, which resizing setting makes the element stretch to occupy all available width within its parent container?** - A) Fixed width - B) Hug contents - C) Fill container - D) Scale proportionally * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** **Fill container** instructs the child element to expand dynamically to fill the available space allocated by its parent Auto Layout container. --- ### Question 5 **What tool in Figma allows frontend engineers to inspect CSS box-model specs, copy design tokens, and view component properties without editing rights?** - A) Design Mode - B) Dev Mode - C) Vector Pen - D) FigJam Whiteboard * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Figma's Dev Mode provides dedicated developer-centric tools: unit switching (px to rem), CSS code snippets, asset export, and change diffing.

lessons.description:
## First Understanding

- **Morph** transitions animate objects between slides — text and images glide instead of jumping.
- Animations should *sequence attention*, not decorate; entrance + emphasis is usually enough.
- Keyboard shortcuts are the pro speed multiplier (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Shift+arrow nudge).## First Understanding

- **Morph** transitions animate objects between slides — text and images glide instead of jumping.
- Animations should *sequence attention*, not decorate; entrance + emphasis is usually enough.
- Keyboard shortcuts are the pro speed multiplier (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Shift+arrow nudge).Motion is polish — done right it makes you look like a pro.

## The Morph transition
1. Duplicate a slide (Ctrl+D)
2. Move/resize an object on the copy
3. Transitions → Morph

```diagram
  Slide 5:  ● logo (small, left)
  Slide 6:  ● logo (large, center)
  Transition: Morph → smooth cinematic zoom
```

## Shortcuts that save hours
| Shortcut | Action |
| -------- | ------ |
| Ctrl+M | new slide |
| Ctrl+D | duplicate slide/object |
| F5 | start show from start |
| Shift+F5 | start from current slide |
| Alt+Shift+↑/↓ | promote/demote outline |
| B / W | black / white screen during show |

> [!tip] Animation ≠ decoration: use Entrance for points you discuss, and nothing else. Subtle beats flashy.

## Suggestions and Tips

- Duplicate a slide and move objects — Morph animates the difference. Magic.
- Use `Fade` as the default transition; reserving Morph for key moments keeps it impactful.
- Set the same object position/size across slides to keep videos and demos stable.

lessons.title: Power Query — Cleaning Like a Pro
lessons.description:
## First Understanding

- **Power Query** records every transformation as **steps** — your cleaning runs forever, unattended.
- Promote headers, filter rows, merge and split columns — all recorded, all repeatable.
- The M language behind it is optional — 90% of work is point-and-click.## First Understanding

- **Power Query** records every transformation as **steps** — your cleaning runs forever, unattended.
- Promote headers, filter rows, merge and split columns — all recorded, all repeatable.
- The M language behind it is optional — 90% of work is point-and-click.80% of analysis time is cleaning data. Power Query does it without code.

## The 10 essential transforms
| Transform | How |
| --------- | --- |
| Remove columns | Right-click → Remove |
| Remove blanks | Filter arrows → deselect (blank) |
| Split column | Split Column → by delimiter |
| Fix data type | Column header icon → Text/Number/Date |
| Fill down | Transform → Fill → Down (for merged cells) |
| Unpivot | Select ID column → Unpivot Other Columns |
| Merge | Home → Merge Queries (join) |
| Append | Home → Append (stack rows) |
| Add column from examples | Add Column → Column From Examples |
| Replace values | Transform → Replace Values |

## Star schema — the professional model
```diagram
        Fact: Sales
        (date_id, product_id, amount)
           │            │
      Date table   Product table
      (dimension)   (dimension)
```

> [!tip] Never merge dimensions into facts. A separate Date table (Modeling → New Table) unlocks all time intelligence.

## Suggestions and Tips

- Rename steps like `Promoted Headers`, `Removed Dupes` — future-you will thank you.
- Never clean in Excel and re-import; that breaks the automated pipeline.
- Use the `First Row` / `Use Headers` toggles instead of manual typing when possible.

lessons.title: How Websites Actually Work
lessons.description: The request–response journey, browsers, and the three languages of the web.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Every website is a conversation: your **browser asks** for files, a **server answers** — no code required to understand this flow.
- Three languages split the work: **HTML** is the content, **CSS** is the looks, **JavaScript** is the behavior.
- You never see the raw files — the browser translates them into the page you interact with.## First Understanding

- Every website is a conversation: your **browser asks** for files, a **server answers** — no code required to understand this flow.
- Three languages split the work: **HTML** is the content, **CSS** is the looks, **JavaScript** is the behavior.
- You never see the raw files — the browser translates them into the page you interact with.
> [!tip] **No code needed yet.** This lesson is a map — read it, then move on.

Every website you have ever opened follows the exact same journey. A **browser** (Chrome, Edge, Safari) is a translator: it reads text files and turns them into the beautiful page you see.

## The journey of a page

```diagram
  YOU                          SERVER
  (browser)                    (host computer)
    |                              |
    | 1. type learnifyai.in        |
    |------------------------------>|
    |                              | 2. finds the page files
    | 3. sends back HTML, CSS, JS  |
    |<------------------------------|
    | 4. browser draws the page    |
    |                              |
```

## The three languages

Every web page is made of exactly three languages. Together they are the whole web:

| Language | What it does | Analogy |
| -------- | ------------ | ------- |
| **HTML** | Structure — headings, text, images, buttons | The skeleton of a body |
| **CSS** | Style — colors, spacing, fonts, layout | The clothes and makeup |
| **JavaScript** | Behavior — clicks, animation, math, logic | The muscles that move |

> [!warning] HTML is not a programming language. HTML has no logic — it cannot "decide" anything. JavaScript does the thinking.

## Key ideas to remember

1. **HTML = content**, **CSS = looks**, **JavaScript = behavior**.
2. The browser always receives the files — the server never renders for you.
3. You can see the code of any page: right-click → **Inspect** (or Ctrl+Shift+I).

## Quick Check

```quiz
Q: Which language decides what happens when a user clicks a button?
A. HTML
B. CSS
C. JavaScript
D. The server
Correct: C
Explain: JavaScript runs in the browser and handles interactions.
```

> [!info] In later lessons you will run all three languages in the built-in IDE — no installations needed.

## Suggestions and Tips

- Right-click any page → **Inspect** to see exactly which HTML, CSS and JS built it — it's free education.
- Don't memorise code yet; memorise the *roles* of each language first.
- Bookmark this lesson's diagram — it's the map for everything that follows.

A) To compress image files for web export. - B) To group related component states (e.g. Default, Hover, Focused, Disabled, Error) under a single master component set for clean design system management. - C) To translate copy into multiple languages automatically. - D) To convert Figma files into Adobe Photoshop format. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Variants allow designers to organize multiple visual states (like buttons in primary, secondary, danger, or hover/active) into one unified component with toggles in the right inspector. --- ### Question 2 **Which Figma component property allows designers to toggle the visibility of a layer (like an icon in a button) on or off from the properties panel without detaching the instance?** - A) Text Property - B) Boolean Property - C) Instance Swap Property - D) Variant Property * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** A **Boolean Property** exposes a True/False switch in the inspector that controls whether a sub-layer (e.g., a left icon or badge) is visible or hidden. --- ### Question 3 **In Figma prototyping, which transition type intelligently matches layer names between two frames to animate position, scale, and opacity differences smoothly?** - A) Instant - B) Dissolve - C) Smart Animate - D) Push * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** **Smart Animate** detects layers with identical names across starting and ending frames and automatically calculates intermediate frames for position, size, rotation, and opacity. --- ### Question 4 **What does the "Auto Layout Wrap" feature in Figma accomplish?** - A) It wraps long text inside a single line. - B) It allows child items in an Auto Layout container to wrap onto a new row or column when they exceed the container width, mimicking CSS `flex-wrap: wrap`. - C) It wraps images in a circular mask. - D) It encrypts the Figma file for export. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Auto Layout Wrap mirrors CSS `flex-wrap`, automatically moving items that exceed container width to the next line—ideal for tag clouds, skill badges, and responsive grids. --- ### Question 5 **What is the primary danger of "Detaching an Instance" (`Ctrl + Alt + B` / `Cmd + Option + B`) in a team design system?** - A) It deletes the master component from the file. - B) The layer permanently breaks its connection to the master component, meaning future brand updates, color changes, and bug fixes will never propagate to that element. - C) It crashes Figma's cloud servers. - D) It locks the layer from being edited. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Detaching an instance severs the link to the design system. If the design system changes, detached instances remain stale, creating design debt and inconsistencies.

# Practice Quiz: Progressive Web Applications (PWA)
**Practice Quiz · 10 Minutes · 5 Questions**

Assess your knowledge of service workers, manifest requirements, offline caching strategies, and native device capabilities.

---

### Question 1
**Where do Service Workers execute within the browser runtime?**
- A) In the main UI thread blocking user interactions.
- B) On a separate background worker thread completely independent of web page DOM access.
- C) Inside the server database engine.
- D) Within an iframe on the user's desktop.
* **Correct Answer:** B
* **Explanation:** Service workers run in an isolated background thread. Because they cannot access the DOM directly, they communicate with web pages using the `postMessage` API, ensuring smooth, non-blocking UI performance.

---

### Question 2
**Which caching strategy delivers immediate zero-latency load from the local cache while simultaneously updating the cache with fresh network data for the next visit?**
- A) Cache Only
- B) Network Only
- C) Stale-While-Revalidate
- D) Network First
* **Correct Answer:** C
* **Explanation:** Stale-While-Revalidate serves cached content immediately to the user while asynchronously dispatching a network request to update the cache with fresh data in the background.

---

### Question 3
**Which manifest display mode hides the browser address bar and navigation controls, providing a true native full-screen app appearance?**
- A) `browser`
- B) `minimal-ui`
- C) `standalone`
- D) `inline`
* **Correct Answer:** C
* **Explanation:** `"display": "standalone"` gives the installed web app its own dedicated application window without the browser URL bar or back/forward buttons.

---

### Question 4
**Why is HTTPS an absolute non-negotiable prerequisite for running Service Workers in production?**
- A) HTTPS reduces the file size of images.
- B) Because Service Workers can intercept, inspect, and modify network requests, allowing HTTP would expose users to devastating Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) attacks.
- C) HTTPS is required only for Google Chrome.
- D) Service workers cannot run on local development machines.
* **Correct Answer:** B
* **Explanation:** A service worker has powerful proxy privileges to intercept all network traffic. On unencrypted connections, an attacker could inject malicious scripts permanently into the cache.

---

### Question 5
**Which audit tool built directly into Chrome DevTools allows developers to verify if a site meets all PWA installability criteria?**
- A) Network Tab
- B) Lighthouse
- C) Memory Tab
- D) Elements Inspector
* **Correct Answer:** B
* **Explanation:** Google Lighthouse audits progressive web apps against PWA criteria: installability, service worker registration, offline response, and splash screen support.

lessons.title: Templates & innerHTML
lessons.description: Render lists and cards with template literals — safely.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding - Template literals (backticks + `${}`) embed values into strings cleanly. - Building markup with templates + `innerHTML` renders whole lists in one go. - Render-then-attach: build the HTML string, set it once, then attach listeners — never in a loop. ## Rendering a list ```js const apps = ["Notion", "Figma", "VS Code"]; const listHtml = apps .map(app => `
  • ${app}
    • `) .join(""); document.getElementById("apps").innerHTML = `
      ${listHtml}
    `; ``` > [!info] Why .join("") > `map` returns an array; `innerHTML` needs a string. `.join("")` merges the items with no separator — one expression, no loops. ## Rendering cards with data ```js const projects = [ { title: "Business Card", tech: "HTML/CSS" }, { title: "Counter App", tech: "JavaScript" }, ]; const cards = projects.map(p => `

    ${p.title}

    Built with ${p.tech}

    `).join(""); document.querySelector("#projects").innerHTML = cards; ``` > [!warning] Only interpolate trusted data > If `p.title` came from a user, `${p.title}` could inject HTML. Escape `<` and `>` (or use textContent) for anything user-supplied. ## Attach events after render ```js document.querySelectorAll(".project").forEach(card => { card.addEventListener("click", () => card.classList.toggle("open")); }); ``` > [!tip] Delegation instead > One listener on the container using `e.target.closest(".project")` beats N listeners on N cards — it survives re-renders automatically. ```diagram data array | v map -> template literals -> array of html strings | v .join("") -> one big string | v container.innerHTML = string (one DOM write) ``` ```quiz Q: What does ${p.tech} inside a template literal do? A. Escapes the string B. Inserts the value of p.tech C. Creates a comment D. Nothing Correct: B Explain: ${expression} evaluates the expression and inserts its string value into the template. ``` ## Suggestions and Tips - One `innerHTML` assignment per render — touching the DOM 100 times in a loop is slow. - Always `console.log(listHtml)` once before wiring it in; you'll catch typos instantly. - Combine with `filter` to render subsets: `data.filter(...).map(...)`.

# Getting Started with Figma and its Features
**Reading & Practical Guide · 10 Minutes**

Figma has revolutionized UI/UX engineering by unifying vector design, interactive prototyping, and design system governance into a real-time collaborative cloud platform.

---

## The 4 Core Workspaces of Figma...
lessons.content_md:
# Getting Started with Figma and its Features **Reading & Practical Guide · 10 Minutes** Figma has revolutionized UI/UX engineering by unifying vector design, interactive prototyping, and design system governance into a real-time collaborative cloud platform. --- ## The 4 Core Workspaces of Figma 1. **Design Canvas:** Infinite 2D space where frames, components, and artboards reside. 2. **FigJam:** Digital whiteboard designed for brainstorming, user story mapping, and sprint retrospectives. 3. **Figma Community:** Open-source ecosystem of design systems, icon packs, and automation plugins. 4. **Dev Mode:** Specialized inspection environment for frontend engineers to view CSS properties, box-model spacing, and token variables. --- ## The 8 Foundational Figma Concepts * **Frames:** Unlike simple bounding boxes, Frames represent screens or containers with clipping, auto layout, and responsive resizing rules. * **Components & Instances:** Master components (`❖`) define source properties; instances (`◇`) inherit updates globally. * **Auto Layout (Flexbox in Design):** Organizes elements into vertical or horizontal stacks with fluid padding, gap, and distribution rules. * **Variables & Tokens:** Centralized variables for colors, typography sizes, corner radii, and spacing. * **Constraints:** Tells elements how to behave when a parent frame is resized (e.g., Pin to Left, Pin to Right, Center, Scale). * **Smart Animate:** Automatically interpolates identical layers across screens to produce realistic micro-interactions and transitions. * **Figma Plugins:** Community utilities that automate asset generation, contrast auditing, and content population. * **Version History:** Automatic cloud checkpoints allowing teams to rollback or branch design changes safely.

lessons.content_md:
# Hands-on Lab: Design a Progressive Web App (PWA) **Lab Assignment · 25 Minutes · Modern Web Architecture** Progressive Web Applications combine the broad reach of the web with the deep engagement, offline reliability, and fast performance of native mobile applications. --- ### Lab Objectives 1. Formulate the Web App Manifest configuration (`manifest.webmanifest`). 2. Design PWA App Shell architecture with offline fallback and skeleton states. 3. Configure Service Worker caching strategies: Cache First, Network First, and Stale-While-Revalidate. 4. Verify PWA installability using the Chrome DevTools Application & Lighthouse audits. --- ### Architectural Blueprint: The PWA Triangle ``` +--------------------------------------------------------------+ | PWA CORE TRIANGLE | +--------------------------------------------------------------+ | | | [ 1. Web App Manifest ] | | - App Name, Icons, Theme Colors, Start URL | | - Standalone Display Mode (No browser URL bar) | | | | [ 2. Service Worker (Offline Engine) ] | | - Background worker thread intercepting network fetch | | - Caching static assets & offline fallbacks | | - Web Push Notifications | | | | [ 3. HTTPS Secure Context ] | | - Encrypted transmission required for Service Workers | | | +--------------------------------------------------------------+ ``` --- ### Step-by-Step Exercise #### Step 1: Create a Production Web App Manifest ```json { "name": "Learnify AI Learning Platform", "short_name": "Learnify AI", "start_url": "/", "display": "standalone", "background_color": "#09090b", "theme_color": "#2563eb", "icons": [ { "src": "/icons/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" }, { "src": "/icons/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "any maskable" } ] } ``` #### Step 2: Implement a Caching Strategy * **Cache First (Static Assets):** Fonts, icons, brand logos, pre-compiled bundles. * **Network First with Cache Fallback (User Profile & Dynamic Data):** Course progress, certificates, quiz attempts. * **Stale-While-Revalidate (Catalog & Course Feeds):** Instant render from cache while fetching latest updates in the background. --- ### Lab Submission Deliverables - [ ] Completed `manifest.webmanifest` JSON snippet for your portfolio or capstone app. - [ ] Definition of which caching strategy fits Course Video Thumbnails vs. Real-time Chat.

lessons.title: Text Contrast, Color & Fonts
lessons.description: Readable type and accessible color — the 30-60-10 rule in action.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- **Contrast is accessibility**: normal text needs a 4.5:1 ratio against its background; large text 3:1.
- Font size in the range 16–18px with line-height 1.5–1.7 is the comfortable reading zone.
- The **60-30-10 rule** keeps palettes calm: 60% dominant, 30% secondary, 10% accent.

## Check contrast like a pro

| Pairing | Ratio | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `#111827` on `#ffffff` | 16:1 | Excellent |
| `#94a3b8` on `#ffffff` | 2.7:1 | Fails — too light |
| `#f8fafc` on `#1e293b` | 13:1 | Excellent (dark mode) |
| `#f87171` on `#ffffff` | 3.2:1 | OK only for large text |

> [!warning] The #94a3b8 trap
> Light gray text on white looks elegant and fails every audit. If it's body copy, darken it to `#475569` or darker.

## A palette that works

```css
:root {
  --dominant: #f8fafc;   /* 60% — page background   */
  --secondary: #e2e8f0;  /* 30% — cards, sections   */
  --accent: #2563eb;     /* 10% — buttons, links    */
  --ink: #0f172a;        /* text on light           */
  --ink-muted: #475569;  /* secondary text (passes) */
}

body {
  font-family: system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  font-size: 1.0625rem;      /* 17px — comfortable */
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: var(--ink);
  background: var(--dominant);
}
```

> [!tip] system-ui fonts
> `system-ui` uses the device's native font — zero download, perfect rendering, no FOUT (flash of unstyled text).

```diagram
  60%  ██████████████  background (dominant)
  30%  ████████       cards, nav, sections
  10%  ███            buttons, links, highlights
```

```quiz
Q: What is the minimum contrast ratio for normal-size text?
A. 2:1
B. 3:1
C. 4.5:1
D. 7:1
Correct: C
Explain: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text; large text (24px+) may use 3:1.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Test palettes with a contrast checker (web.dev or browser DevTools) before shipping.
- Never style text with the same gray as placeholder/hint color — users will skip it.
- Accent color is for interactive things; muted neutrals carry the reading text.

lessons.description:
# Module 3 Graded Quiz: UI Design with Figma
**Graded Assessment · 15 Minutes · 6 Questions · 80% to Pass**

Demonstrate comprehensive proficiency in Figma components, auto layout physics, component variants, and interactive prototyping.

---

### Question 1
**When creating an 8pt Grid design system...
lessons.content_md:
# Module 3 Graded Quiz: UI Design with Figma **Graded Assessment · 15 Minutes · 6 Questions · 80% to Pass** Demonstrate comprehensive proficiency in Figma components, auto layout physics, component variants, and interactive prototyping. --- ### Question 1 **When creating an 8pt Grid design system, what should your spacing, padding, and dimension values ideally be?** - A) Any arbitrary odd number like 13px, 17px, 21px. - B) Multiples of 8 (e.g., 8px, 16px, 24px, 32px, 48px, 64px) with occasional 4px half-steps for micro-spacing. - C) Exactly 10px, 20px, 30px, 40px. - D) Values determined entirely by browser randomizers. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** The 8pt grid system enforces visual rhythm and mathematical predictability across all screen densities (1x, 2x, 3x displays), minimizing rendering rounding errors. --- ### Question 2 **A designer wants a navigation header to remain locked at the top of the mobile viewport while the user scrolls down the page in Figma prototype mode. Which setting must be enabled on the header frame?** - A) Hug contents - B) "Fix position when scrolling" (or "Stay in place") - C) Detach instance - D) Smart Animate * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** "Fix position when scrolling" pins the layer to the prototype viewport coordinates, ensuring it remains visible regardless of page scroll position. --- ### Question 3 **What is the role of Design Tokens in modern design systems?** - A) They are cryptocurrency coins used to purchase Figma plugins. - B) They are platform-agnostic design variables (colors, typography, spacing, shadows) stored as key-value pairs that translate design decisions directly into CSS, iOS, and Android code. - C) They are security passwords for Figma files. - D) They are vector icons used exclusively in wireframing. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Design tokens bridge the gap between design and development by codifying decisions (e.g. `color-primary-500: #2563EB`) into reusable variables consumed by code. --- ### Question 4 **In Figma, when setting up an interactive hover state on a button component, where should the interaction be connected?** - A) Inside the master component set between the "Default" variant and the "Hover" variant using the "While hovering" trigger. - B) On every single screen where the button is pasted throughout the file. - C) In the CSS style sheet. - D) Inside the file comment thread. * **Correct Answer:** A * **Explanation:** Creating component-level interactions (Interactive Components) between variants ensures that every instance in your prototype automatically inherits the hover interaction. --- ### Question 5 **Which constraint setting ensures that a floating action button (FAB) stays 24px from the bottom-right corner of a screen when viewed on different phone sizes?** - A) Top and Left - B) Center and Center - C) Bottom and Right - D) Scale and Scale * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** Pinning constraints to **Right** and **Bottom** maintains fixed 24px margins relative to the right and bottom edges of the parent frame as it resizes. --- ### Question 6 **What is the primary benefit of using "Auto Layout Min/Max Width" in responsive card design?** - A) It prevents cards from becoming unreadably narrow on small phones or excessively stretched on ultrawide monitors. - B) It forces text to render in uppercase. - C) It disables dark mode automatically. - D) It exports vector SVG files. * **Correct Answer:** A * **Explanation:** Setting min-width and max-width on an Auto Layout component guarantees that fluid layouts remain within ergonomically sound bounds across all device form factors.

Code & Dev Handoff Readiness (25 Points) - Clear layer naming hierarchy (e.g. `Card / Course / Default` rather than `Frame 492`). - Exportable SVG icons and web-optimized assets prepared. - Complete documentation of spacing tokens and typography scale.

# Module 4 Graded Final Comprehensive Assessment **Final Exam · 20 Minutes · 8 Questions · 80% Passing Grade** This comprehensive final assessment evaluates your mastery across all four course modules: UX Strategy, Visual Design, Responsive/PWA Architecture, and Figma Prototyping. --- ### Question 1 **What is the core distinction between Low-Fidelity and High-Fidelity prototypes?** - A) Low-fidelity prototypes are coded in Python; high-fidelity are in JavaScript. - B) Low-fidelity prototypes focus on user flow and layout structure using basic shapes and grayscale; high-fidelity prototypes incorporate production-ready typography, branding, actual copy, and realistic micro-interactions. - C) Low-fidelity prototypes are only used after a product launches. - D) High-fidelity prototypes never require user testing. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Low-fidelity wireframes strip away cosmetic distractions to test core navigation and structure, while high-fidelity prototypes test emotional resonance, visual hierarchy, and precise interaction timing. --- ### Question 2 **Under the Gestalt law of Common Region, how do users perceive elements enclosed within a visible border or background card?** - A) As unrelated individual items. - B) As belonging to a single, unified conceptual group. - C) As broken links. - D) As inactive disabled elements. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** The principle of Common Region demonstrates that enclosing items within a shared border or background surface creates an immediate visual association that they belong to the same category. --- ### Question 3 **Which metric in Google Core Web Vitals measures visual stability by tracking unexpected layout shifts during page load?** - A) LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) - B) INP (Interaction to Next Paint) - C) CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) - D) TTFB (Time to First Byte) * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures unexpected shifts in visual content as images, fonts, or ads load, directly impacting user frustration. --- ### Question 4 **In Figma, how does "Hug contents" differ from "Fill container"?** - A) "Hug contents" shrinks the container to tightly fit the size of its children; "Fill container" stretches the element to occupy the full available width of its parent container. - B) "Hug contents" is for images only. - C) "Fill container" deletes the padding. - D) They are identical in every way. * **Correct Answer:** A * **Explanation:** In Auto Layout, "Hug" sets dimensions determined by the content inside, while "Fill" tells the layer to expand into whatever space the parent offers. --- ### Question 5 **What is the minimum recommended touch target size specified by Google's Material Design guidelines for mobile user interfaces?** - A) 24 x 24 dp - B) 32 x 32 dp - C) 48 x 48 dp - D) 96 x 96 dp * **Correct Answer:** C * **Explanation:** Material Design guidelines recommend at least 48x48 dp with adequate spacing to prevent accidental mis-taps on touchscreens. --- ### Question 6 **Which accessibility standard must be met to ensure text is legible for users with moderate vision loss (WCAG 2.1 AA)?** - A) 1.5:1 for all text - B) 4.5:1 for normal body text, and 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold) - C) 10:1 for everything - D) 2.0:1 for links * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** WCAG 2.1 Level AA establishes a 4.5:1 minimum contrast ratio for normal text and 3:1 for large typography against their backgrounds. --- ### Question 7 **Why are Design Tokens considered the gold standard for maintaining consistency between Figma and production code?** - A) They eliminate the need for designers and developers to communicate. - B) They store design decisions (colors, radii, spacing, font weights) in platform-agnostic format, allowing automatic sync to CSS variables, Tailwind themes, and mobile style sheets. - C) They automatically write server SQL databases. - D) They convert vector icons into JPEG images. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** Tokens act as the single source of truth: when a token value is updated, it propagates automatically across both Figma libraries and production codebases. --- ### Question 8 **In Progressive Web Applications, what is the role of the Web App Manifest file?** - A) It compiles React components into binary code. - B) It provides metadata (app name, start URL, theme color, icons, display mode) that tells the operating system how to install and launch the web app. - C) It connects the client to a payment gateway. - D) It tracks user analytics. * **Correct Answer:** B * **Explanation:** The Web App Manifest (`manifest.webmanifest`) informs browsers how your PWA should present itself on mobile or desktop home screens and application launchers.

lessons.title: Copilot & AI Pair Programming
lessons.description: AI-assisted coding is now the default — here's how to stay in control.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- AI completions (Copilot-style) now ship inside VS Code and most editors — knowing how to steer them is a job skill.
- The best prompt is a clear intent: describe the function in a comment, and the model completes it.
- AI suggests; you review. The 2026 skill is critical review, not memorising libraries.

## The pattern

```
// TODO comment -> describes intent:
// function that counts words in a string, ignoring punctuation
```

> [!info] How pros use it
> Write the intent as a comment or function name, accept the suggestion, then immediately read it critically: edge cases (empty input), performance, and security all stay human responsibilities.

## Your daily loop

1. Let the AI complete boilerplate (imports, repetitive lines) — you keep the design.
2. Ask it to explain code you didn't write: select code → "Explain this" in the AI chat.
3. Use it to generate tests — but review them; generated tests can miss the real bug.

> [!warning] The blind-accept trap
> Accepting every suggestion is how bugs become invisible. Suggestion speed ≠ correctness. Verify before committing.

> [!tip] Commit messages too
> AI writes decent commit messages from your diff — saves minutes daily and documents your work.

```quiz
Q: What is the 2026 professional skill when using AI code suggestions?
A. Accepting suggestions faster
B. Critically reviewing every suggestion
C. Writing longer prompts
D. Avoiding AI entirely
Correct: B
Explain: AI boosts speed; humans own correctness, security and intent.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Practise writing intent comments: if the AI can't complete them, your intent wasn't clear.
- Never paste proprietary code into a free AI tool — check your employer's policy first.
- Turn suggestions OFF during deep problem-solving, ON during implementation.

lessons.title: Claude & GPT at Work in 2026
lessons.description: What the flagship models are actually good at — and where they still fail.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Both Claude and GPT-class models are now fast, cheap and multimodal (text, images, files).
- Their sweet spot: drafting, restructuring, explaining, summarising, and paired coding.
- Their weak spot: confident-but-wrong facts ("hallucination") and invented references.

## Choose by job

| Task | Why they're strong | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Drafting emails/docs | Instantly solid structure and tone | Unverified specifics |
| Explaining concepts | Patient, tailored, interactive | Overconfidence |
| Coding with context | Whole-file awareness, refactors | Stale library syntax |
| Data analysis | Reads CSV/XLSX, writes scripts | Silent assumptions |

> [!info] The verification habit
> Treat every output as a strong first draft. Facts, links and numbers need checking — this is your job, forever.

## A prompt that gets results

```
You are a senior [role]. Here is my context: [paste relevant info].
Task: [one clear deliverable]. Constraints: [length, tone, audience].
Give me: [exact format, e.g. bullet list + one-paragraph summary].
```

> [!tip] Iterate, don't retype
> The first answer is a draft. Reply "Make it shorter, more direct, for beginners" — steering beats regenerating.

```quiz
Q: What should you do with a citation a model just invented?
A. Use it anyway
B. Verify it before including it
C. Hide the source
D. Ask it to apologise
Correct: B
Explain: Models can invent plausible references. Verification is mandatory for anything factual.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Practise one workflow: paste a messy brief, ask for a structured plan, refine twice.
- Ask for the model's reasoning when the answer surprises you — then judge the logic.
- Know your data policy: never paste personal or company-confidential text into consumer tools.

lessons.title: Python + AI Tooling in 2026
lessons.description: The language behind the AI boom — and how beginners ride it.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Python powers AI/ML libraries, data pipelines, automation and scripting — its job market keeps growing.
- The beginner-friendly path: Python fundamentals → automation scripts → data with pandas → AI APIs.
- You don't need to build models to benefit: calling AI APIs from Python is 15 lines.

## The realistic ladder

```python
# 1. Automate a boring task (files, emails, renames)
# 2. Data wrangling with pandas
# 3. Calling an AI API:

import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/chat",
    json={"prompt": "Summarise this paragraph for me", "max_tokens": 100},
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_KEY"},
    timeout=30,
)
print(response.json()["text"])
```

> [!info] API-first AI
> Most teams integrate AI by calling hosted APIs, not training models. That's Python + requests — achievable at beginner level with the right course.

## What employers ask in 2026

- Scripting and automation (files, scheduling, web scraping basics)
- Data handling: pandas, CSV/Excel, basic visualisation
- Comfort with AI APIs and prompt-driven features
- Testing and clean code habits (the boring wins)

> [!warning] Don't start with frameworks
> FastAPI/Django before fundamentals = confusion. Master plain Python, then add one web framework if you need one.

> [!tip] A fun first project
> Build a script that reads a folder of files and renames them by a rule. Ten lines, instant satisfaction, real job skill.

```quiz
Q: Which is the best first Python project for a beginner in 2026?
A. A machine-learning model from scratch
B. An automation script for a real boring task
C. A compiler
D. A blockchain
Correct: B
Explain: Automating a real task teaches fundamentals and delivers value — the best motivator known.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Pair your course with small scripts you actually need — motivation compounds.
- Learn `pip install` and virtual environments early; every project needs them.
- Read AI-generated code critically: Python's flexibility makes sloppy code easy.

lessons.title: Gemini in Workspace: AI at Your Desk
lessons.description: Summaries, drafts and automation are built into the apps you already use.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Gemini now lives inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Drive and Meet — no separate tool needed.
- Core moves: "Help me write", "Summarise this thread", "Draft reply", "Make a formula".
- The skill is directing it precisely (tone, length, format) and checking the output.

## Everyday AI moves

```
Gmail:  "Summarise this email thread in 3 bullet points."
Docs:   "Help me write a one-page project brief for a client."
Sheets: "Create a formula that totals column B if column A is 'done'."
Meet:   "Take notes and list action items."  (after recording)
```

> [!info] Where it shines
> Long threads, repetitive formatting, meeting notes and first drafts are the sweet spot. Precision work — final numbers, legal language — stays human.

> [!warning] Watch the data
> Workspace AI is only as safe as your domain settings. Don't paste secrets or customer data into AI features without checking policy.

> [!tip] One skill to practise
> Use "Help me write" with a target tone and length for one email a day. In a week, the drafts become genuinely useful.

```diagram
  you ask in plain language
       |
       v
  Gemini reads your doc/thread/meeting context
       |
       v
  draft / summary / formula returned
       |
       v
  YOU review, fix, approve  (the actual job)
```

```quiz
Q: What is the user's job after Gemini drafts something in Workspace?
A. Approve without reading
B. Review, correct and refine
C. Rewrite from scratch always
D. Delete the draft
Correct: B
Explain: AI produces first drafts; humans own accuracy and final judgment.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Try "make it more formal" / "make it friendlier" on the same draft — learn how it steers.
- Gemini in Sheets explains formulas too: ask "what does this formula do?"
- Keep key shortcuts: type "@" in Docs and Sheets to summon the AI chip menu.

lessons.title: AI in Spreadsheets: Formula Help & Copilot
lessons.description: Describe what you want in English — get a formula, a pivot, or an insight.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Copilot (Excel) and Gemini (Sheets) now turn plain English into formulas, pivots and charts.
- The real skill remains understanding the result: what the formula does, and whether it's right.
- AI also explains existing formulas and suggests data patterns — a learning accelerator.

## The English-to-formula workflow

```
"Total sales for March where region = West"
"Flag rows where revenue dropped more than 20% vs last month"
"Show average order value by product category"
```

> [!info] It's still your data
> The AI reads your workbook and writes the calculation. Data errors, missing values and logic mistakes stay yours to catch — verify with spot checks.

## Read formulas, don't memorise

```
=SUMIFS(Total, Region, "West", Month, "March")
=IF(B2/C2 < 0.8, "FLAG", "OK")
=AVERAGEIFS(OrderValue, Category, A2)
```

> [!tip] Ask "explain this"
> Select any scary formula and ask the AI to explain it in plain English. You'll absorb Excel's vocabulary three times faster.

> [!warning] Check the edge cases
> AI formulas can silently assume your data starts at row 2 or that cells are numbers. A quick sum-check catches it.

```quiz
Q: After AI generates a formula, what should you do first?
A. Trust it — AI is accurate
B. Verify it against a known result
C. Hide it in a helper column
D. Rewrite it manually
Correct: B
Explain: Spot-check against a value you computed by hand; AI can misread headers or ranges.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Practise describing a problem in English before reaching for a function — the skill carries over.
- Learn what the generated formula means: each new function learned = permanent skill.
- Use AI to clean messy data (duplicates, inconsistent casing) before analysis.

lessons.title: Power BI & AI: Auto Insights
lessons.description: Copilot-generated dashboards and "explain the trend" questions.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Power BI now includes Copilot: describe a dashboard, ask questions in natural language, get insight explanations.
- "Why is sales down?" returns a narrative with contributing factors — huge for analysis speed.
- The analyst's craft — data quality, KPI choice, story structure — is exactly what AI can't replace.

## AI moves in Power BI

```
"Create a dashboard showing revenue, margin and new customers by quarter."
"Explain the drop in Q3 revenue."           -> narrative + drivers
"Show me the top 5 products by growth."     -> visual, one click
"Summarise this report for a CFO."          -> narrative summary
```

> [!info] Natural-language questions
> The Q&A feature turns typed questions into visuals: "bar chart of orders by month, filtered to India". Think in verbs and fields.

> [!warning] Narrative ≠ proof
> Copilot's explanations are hypotheses from your data. Verify the driver claims with the underlying table before presenting them.

> [!tip] The 5-minute demo skill
> Practise: load sample data → ask for a dashboard → refine with "make it cleaner, add a trend line". It's a portable demo for interviews.

```diagram
  data model (cleaned, shaped)
        |
        v
  ask in English: "why did X fall?"
        |
        v
  Copilot: narrative + candidate drivers
        |
        v
  YOU verify against raw tables -> publish story
```

```quiz
Q: When Copilot explains why sales fell, what must the analyst still do?
A. Nothing — trust it
B. Verify drivers against the raw data
C. Delete the explanation
D. Rebuild the data model
Correct: B
Explain: AI narratives are hypotheses; verification against source data is the analyst's core job.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Keep your data model clean (types, relationships) — AI insight quality depends on it.
- Use "explain" features on dashboards you already understand, to learn what the AI notices.
- Practise writing the question with and without filters — precision in questions = precision in answers.

lessons.title: Word & PPT with Copilot: AI Documents
lessons.description: Draft, design and summarise with AI — then add the human polish.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Microsoft 365 Copilot drafts documents, decks and emails from a prompt — with your content in mind.
- PowerPoint Copilot can generate a whole deck from a Word doc or a one-line brief.
- The premium skill: directing the AI and editing its output into something that sounds like you.

## Document moves

```
Word:  "Draft a one-page proposal for a website redesign, professional tone."
       "Summarise this report into 3 key takeaways."
PowerPoint: "Create a 10-slide deck from the attached Word doc, clean style."
       "Add a comparison slide for option A vs B."
```

> [!info] It reads your context
> Copilot references your document, meeting notes and email — that's why results are better than generic chat. It's also why you should review: context can be stale.

> [!warning] Design language
> AI slides default to generic. Apply your brand theme (colours, fonts) from the design tab afterwards — that's the polish that separates decks.

> [!tip] The two-pass edit
> First pass: cut AI filler. Second pass: add your specifics (names, numbers, opinions). Result: fast + authentically yours.

```quiz
Q: What makes Copilot's document results better than generic chat prompts?
A. It writes faster
B. It references your own files and context
C. It never makes mistakes
D. It checks grammar perfectly
Correct: B
Explain: Copilot grounds answers in your documents, meetings and mail — context beats generic knowledge.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Give every deck a prompt with audience, length and one goal — specificity pays off.
- Use "Rewrite" on your own paragraphs for tone options; steal the best phrasing.
- Always check speaker notes: AI fills them with useful cues you can refine.

lessons.title: Figma AI: Design at Machine Speed
lessons.description: First draft to polished screens with AI — and why craft still wins.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- Figma's AI features turn prompts and screenshots into editable designs and components.
- The workflow: AI produces the first draft, you refine with real craft (spacing, hierarchy, tokens).
- Portfolio expectations moved up: recruiters want polished, systematic design, not just concepts.

## AI workflows

```
"Generate a landing page for a meditation app"   -> editable frames
Paste a screenshot -> "Rebuild this as a component set"
"Make a mobile variant of this desktop screen"
"Clean up the layers / auto-layout this group"
```

> [!info] Editable output
> The point of Figma AI (vs image generators) is that results are real design files — layers, text, styles you can restructure.

> [!warning] Design systems still rule
> AI drafts won't use your tokens, spacing scale or accessibility contrast. Re-apply the system — that's the professional value-add.

> [!tip] The 15-minute portfolio exercise
> Take any app you love → screenshot → rebuild it in Figma with AI help → refine to a component library. Instant portfolio upgrade.

```diagram
  prompt / screenshot
       |
       v
  Figma AI -> editable frames + components
       |
       v
  YOUR craft: tokens, spacing, hierarchy, a11y
       |
       v
  polished, systematic design
```

```quiz
Q: What separates a senior designer's AI workflow from a beginner's?
A. Better prompts only
B. Re-applying craft: systems, tokens and accessibility
C. Faster clicking
D. Using more plugins
Correct: B
Explain: AI speeds the draft; the design system and polish remain human craft.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Always ask for editable frames, not images — the file is the deliverable.
- Rebuild 2–3 real products with AI help to learn what the tool does well.
- Keep a checklist: spacing scale, type scale, contrast, states — apply it to every AI draft.

lessons.title: AI Site Builders vs Templates
lessons.description: When to use a template, when to let AI build, and when to hand-code.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- AI site builders (prompt → full site) are real and fast; templates give you design control.
- Decision framework: speed vs control vs cost — each tool wins in different situations.
- The 2026 advantage: knowing all three, and when to mix them (AI draft → template polish).

## The decision grid

| Goal | Best tool | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Landing page today | AI builder | Instant, zero setup |
| Branded business site | Template + customisation | Design quality + control |
| Portfolio / blog | Template | Focus on content |
| Web app / custom logic | Hand-coded | Full flexibility |
| Internal tool | AI builder or code | Speed wins |

> [!info] The hybrid workflow
> Draft with AI, restructure inside a template's editor, hand-code the touches the tools can't do. Pros mix all three in one project.

> [!warning] The lock-in check
> AI builders can make exporting painful. Before committing, confirm you can export code or content — your site should never be a hostage.

> [!tip] Reuse your Template Mastery skills
> Everything you learned editing templates — sections, themes, responsiveness, publishing — applies unchanged to AI-generated sites.

```quiz
Q: When is an AI site builder the right choice?
A. When you need full backend logic
B. When speed beats custom requirements
C. When you need strict brand control
D. When the site has 50 pages
Correct: B
Explain: AI builders win on speed for simple sites; control and complexity favour templates or code.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Build the same small site three ways (AI builder, template, hand-coded) once — then you'll know each tool's true ceiling.
- Keep a folder of strong template sections to mix into AI outputs.
- Your next project: pick the tool from the grid, then explain why — that's the 2026 planning skill.

lessons.title: How a Web Page Is Built
lessons.description:
## First Understanding

- A page is **three layers**: HTML content, CSS presentation, JS behavior — the browser merges them.
- The browser **requests** files (HTML, CSS, JS, images) and **renders** them into a page.
- You can peek at any site's recipe with **View Source** or DevTools.## First Understanding

- A page is **three layers**: HTML content, CSS presentation, JS behavior — the browser merges them.
- The browser **requests** files (HTML, CSS, JS, images) and **renders** them into a page.
- You can peek at any site's recipe with **View Source** or DevTools.Every page you see starts as plain text. Browsers read that text and paint it as a page.

## The three layers

| Layer | Language | Job |
| ----- | -------- | --- |
| Structure | HTML | Headings, paragraphs, images, links |
| Style | CSS | Colors, spacing, fonts, layout |
| Behavior | JavaScript | Clicks, forms, dynamic content |

```diagram
  HTML text  ──►  Browser engine  ──►  Rendered page
      │              │                      │
      │              └── reads CSS ──────────┘
      └── reads JS → reacts to your clicks
```

> [!tip] You will NOT memorize everything. You will learn where things live and how to look things up — that is what professionals actually do.

## Suggestions and Tips

- Open DevTools (F12) on your favorite site and explore — 10 minutes here beats 10 hours of theory.
- Build the habit of asking *'which layer is this?'* whenever you see a page element.
- Start every project with HTML first, then CSS, then JS — in that order.

- Build the habit of asking *'which layer is this?'* whenever you see a page element.
- Start every project with HTML first, then CSS, then JS — in that order.

lessons.title: 3. How to make the most out of this course
lessons.description: Strategies and best practices for completing exercises, hands-on labs, and quizzes.
lessons.content_md:
**How to make the most out of this course** Welcome to Designing User Interfaces and Experiences (UI/UX). You can expect to spend approximately 2-3 hours per module in this four-week class. Here are some tips regarding self-paced learning and getting the most out of this class. 1\. Familiarize yourself with the course content. Browse the module overviews and objectives to get a feel for the topics presented and the assets associated with the subject of each module. Get accustomed to the presented order of the content. Knowing what topics will be covered next allows you to connect the ideas to form a cohesive whole. 2\. Plan and make a rough timeline for completion. Now that you are familiar with the module’s topics, look at the overall completion time estimates for the assets in the modules. Set a reasonable goal for yourself to complete each module. Determine when you would like to finish the course and schedule time each day to study. 3\. Actively consume each asset. Take notes while watching the instructional videos or download the transcripts and highlight the parts of the narration that you think are most important. Keep engaged by completing all the interactive activities. Take all the practice quizzes. Read all the feedback for correct and incorrect responses. You can retake the practice quizzes until you get all the answers right. Take all the graded quizzes. Incorrect responses will direct you to the video which covers the addressed information. Review the video or the transcript to identify the correct response and ascertain why that answer is correct. Retake graded quizzes until you pass. 4\. Talk to your friends and family about the course. Be accountable and commit to the course by talking to your friends and family. Engage them in conversation when you find a topic that piques your interest or where you think another perspective may be beneficial. 5\. Follow your plan. Now that you have a plan, keep yourself motivated by rewarding yourself as you achieve your goals (2).

lessons.title: Images, Fonts & Brand Colors
lessons.description: Make a template feel like your brand: the 60-30-10 color rule and font pairing.
lessons.content_md:
## First Understanding

- The **60-30-10 rule**: 60% neutral base, 30% secondary, 10% accent — instantly professional palettes.
- Fonts have personality: pair one display font (headings) with one readable font (body).
- Colors, fonts and images are your brand — the fastest way to make a template feel yours.## First Understanding

- The **60-30-10 rule**: 60% neutral base, 30% secondary, 10% accent — instantly professional palettes.
- Fonts have personality: pair one display font (headings) with one readable font (body).
- Colors, fonts and images are your brand — the fastest way to make a template feel yours.
Nothing makes a template feel *yours* faster than your own colors, fonts and imagery. Here is the designer's playbook.

## The 60-30-10 color rule

| Share | Where | Example |
| ----- | ----- | ------- |
| **60%** | Background / dominant color | `#f8fafc` |
| **30%** | Secondary elements (cards, sidebar) | `#e2e8f0` |
| **10%** | Accent — buttons, links, highlights | `#6366f1` |

> [!warning] Never use more than 3–4 colors on a page. The 10% accent is what makes a page look "designed".

## Font pairing that always works

- **Headings:** a strong display font (e.g. *Poppins*, *Space Grotesk*).
- **Body:** a clean readable font (e.g. *Inter*, *system-ui*).
- **Rule:** one display + one body = never more.

## Applying it to a template

```css
:root {
  --bg: #f8fafc;        /* 60%  */
  --panel: #ffffff;     /* 30%  */
  --accent: #6366f1;    /* 10%  */
  --ink: #0f172a;
}

body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--ink); }
button { background: var(--accent); color: white; border: none; padding: 10px 18px; border-radius: 10px; }
```

Using **CSS variables** (the `--name` syntax) means one change re-colors your whole site.

## Quick Check

```quiz
Q: In the 60-30-10 rule, where does your brand's accent color belong?
A. On the whole background
B. On most text
C. On buttons, links and highlights
D. On images only
Correct: C
Explain: The 10% accent is reserved for interactive highlights — it is what makes pages look designed.
```

## Suggestions and Tips

- Steal palettes from real sites (DevTools → color picker) instead of guessing.
- Compress images before uploading — heavy images are the #1 slow-site cause.
- If in doubt, remove one color rather than adding one.

lessons.title: 1. Course Introduction
lessons.description:
Lesson 1: Course Introduction

In this introductory lesson to the Designing User Interfaces and Experiences (UI & UX) course, we will explore the core concepts and fundamental principles of UI and UX design. The primary focus is to provide a comprehensive overview of what UI and UX entail and their importance in creating engaging and user-friendly digital products.

The core concept of this lesson revolves around understanding the differences and interrelations between UI (User Interface) and UX (User Experience) design. UI design focuses on the visual aspects and usability of a product, while UX design encompasses the overall experience a user has when interacting with a product, from the initial stage of awareness to the point of engagement and beyond.

Key Takeaways:

  • Definition and distinction between UI and UX design
  • Importance of UI and UX in digital product development
  • Overview of the design process and methodologies
  • Introduction to design tools and software

Quick Summary:

  1. Introduction to the course and its objectives
  2. Understanding UI and UX design principles
  3. Recognizing the role of UI and UX in enhancing user engagement and satisfaction

This lesson sets the stage for diving deeper into the world of UI and UX design, equipping learners with the foundational knowledge needed to navigate the complexities of designing user interfaces and experiences that are both aesthetically pleasing and highly functional.
